content: The guidelines provide detailed recommendations for the diagnosis of HIV infection, the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for both treatment and prevention of HIV, and the care of individuals living with HIV. These guidelines are structured along the continuum of HIV services, encompassing testing, prevention, treatment, and care. The World Health Organization (WHO) first issued guidelines on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for adults and adolescents with HIV in 2002, followed by guidance on preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV in 2004. In 2006, the guidelines introduced a public health approach, emphasizing simplified and harmonized ART regimens. By 2013, WHO consolidated these and other ARV-related recommendations into a single set of guidelines addressing HIV treatment and prevention across all age groups and populations, based on the continuum of HIV services. The 2016 edition updates the 2013 consolidated guidelines following an extensive review of evidence and consultations conducted in mid-2015. These updates were shared at the end of 2015 and are now published in full. The revised guidelines aim to simplify and harmonize care for all age groups and populations, addressing both clinical and operational aspects of HIV management. This approach ensures that all guidelines impacting the continuum of HIV care are aligned with a public health framework. Since 2013, significant advancements have occurred in the field of HIV. Evidence strongly supports the initiation of ART at earlier stages, which leads to improved clinical outcomes for people living with HIV compared to delayed treatment. Additionally, safer and more effective ARV drugs are now available, including integrase inhibitors, which are becoming more affordable for lowand middle-income countries. Many countries are transitioning to providing lifelong ART to all pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 cell count, and are adopting viral load testing as the preferred method for monitoring ART effectiveness. New point-of-care viral load testing technologies further enhance this approach. In terms of prevention, clinical trials have confirmed the efficacy of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, alone or in combination with emtricitabine, as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV acquisition across diverse settings and populations. Innovative HIV testing strategies, such as home testing, community-based testing, and self-testing, are being implemented to expand access to diagnosis. The opportunity to use ARV drugs more effectively for both treatment and prevention is rapidly growing. While countries are at varying stages of ART coverage and implementation of the 2013 guidelines, there is a clear trend toward earlier treatment initiation and expanded use of ARV drugs for prevention to achieve greater impact. This expansion is accompanied by a strong emphasis on increasing access to HIV testing, treatment, and prevention in high-burden settings and among vulnerable populations. Efforts to address stigma and discrimination are also critical to maintaining focus and accelerating the response to the epidemic. The 2016 guidelines introduce several new recommendations, including the provision of lifelong ART to all children, adolescents, and adults living with HIV, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 cell count. WHO has also expanded its earlier recommendations to offer PrEP to individuals at substantial risk of acquiring HIV. Alternative first-line treatment regimens are recommended, including the use of integrase inhibitors in resource-limited settings and reduced dosages of efavirenz to improve tolerability and reduce costs. The new recommendations on when to start ART and the use of PrEP, due to their anticipated public health impact, were released in September 2015. Implementing these recommendations at national and global levels will have significant implications for program priorities, funding, and service delivery. Operational guidance is included to assist countries in adopting new approaches and strengthening the treatment cascade. The guidelines include ten new recommendations aimed at improving the quality and efficiency of services for people living with HIV. Universal eligibility for ART will result in earlier treatment initiation for more individuals. WHO emphasizes the need for differentiated care approaches for stable ART patients, such as reducing clinic visit frequency and implementing community-based ART distribution. These efficiencies are essential for managing the growing number of people receiving ART in high-burden settings and reducing the burden on both patients and healthcare facilities. The second edition of the consolidated guidelines is being published in a changing global context for HIV and broader health priorities. The goal of providing HIV treatment to 15 million people by the end of 2015 has been achieved. From 2016 onward, countries must accelerate efforts to meet the ambitious Fast-Track targets for 2020, including major reductions in HIV-related deaths and achieving the 90–90–90 treatment targets: ensuring that 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed are accessing treatment, and 90% of those on treatment achieve viral suppression. The clinical and operational recommendations in these guidelines, along with consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services and strategic information published in 2015, are expected to contribute significantly to achieving these goals in the coming years. They will also support other health and development priorities outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals. The forthcoming Global Health Sector Strategy on HIV 2016–2021 outlines WHO’s role in achieving the HIVand health-related Sustainable Development Goals. This edition of the guidelines was revised in accordance with procedures established by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. New clinical and operational recommendations are based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to evidence review. Modeling, expert consultations, and country case studies have informed the guidelines, while identifying key knowledge gaps to guide future HIV research agendas. The primary audience for these guidelines includes national HIV program managers in lowand middle-income countries. They will also serve as a valuable resource for clinicians, policymakers, development agencies, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and other implementing partners. Additionally, the guidelines will benefit people living with HIV, communities, and civil society organizations, who must be meaningfully engaged to ensure successful implementation.
